scope.start: 8a.4: Rami bar Chama's inference that one who lifts a found item for another acquires it for him
scope.end: 8b.12: the Mishnah's rider as a second kind of *manhig*

sections.title: Can One Lift a Found Item to Acquire It for Someone Else?
sections.gist: Rami bar Chama learns from the garment Mishnah that one who lifts a found item for another acquires it for him. Otherwise two who lift it together would each have lifted only half, and neither would acquire. Rava holds that the Mishnah works only by *miggo*: one who acquires for himself carries his partner along. He proves this from partners who steal, then tests it on a *cheresh* and a *pikeach* who lift a find together.

children.title: Rami bar Chama: Two Who Lift Together Prove One Can Acquire for Another
children.gist: Rami bar Chama rules that one who lifts a found item for another acquires it for him. Two who lift a garment together each lift only part, so the Mishnah's ruling that they divide it shows each is acquiring the other's part for him.

bullets.text: Rami bar Chama infers from the Mishnah of two holding a garment: one who performs *hagbahah* (lifting, the act that acquires a movable object) on a found item on behalf of another acquires it for that person.

His reasoning: when two lift a garment together, each lifts only his own part. If lifting for another did not acquire, each part would count as though it still lay on the ground, neither would acquire, and a third party who took it could keep it. Since the Mishnah has them divide it, each must be acquiring the other's part for him.

Why is this new? *Zakhin le'adam she'lo be'fanav* (one may acquire a benefit for a person in his absence) is well established. But taking a find for someone shuts out everyone else who might have taken it, and one might think a person may do that only for himself, not for another at their expense.
Neither finder means to give anything away. But since the *kinyan* works only if each also lifts for the other, we assume that is what each is doing.

children.title: Rava: Lifting for Another Works Only by *Miggo*
children.gist: Rava holds that one who lifts a find solely for another does not acquire it for him. In the Mishnah each acquires the other's part because he is acquiring for himself, and Rava proves the mechanism from partners who steal, against an agent sent to steal.

bullets.text: Rava rejects the proof: one who lifts a found item solely for another does not acquire it for him. In the Mishnah each acquires the other's part through *miggo* (since): since he acquires his own part for himself, he acquires the other part for his fellow too.

Rava's evidence. One who tells an agent to go steal for him is exempt when the agent steals, by *ein shaliach li'dvar aveirah* (there is no agency for a transgression): the agent's act is not counted as the sender's.

Yet partners who steal together are both liable, even if only one of them lifted the item. The reason must be that the one who lifted it, since he acquires for himself, acquires for his partner as well, and the Gemara concludes that this is so.

So an act a man does for himself can carry another along, while an act done purely for someone else may not. That leaves open whether one who stands to gain nothing can take a find for another, which is just where shutting out others is the concern.

children.title: A *Cheresh* and a *Pikeach* Lift a Found Item Together
children.gist: Rava applies *miggo* to a *cheresh* and a *pikeach* who lift a find together. The Gemara revises his ruling twice, from both acquiring, to the *cheresh* alone, to neither, since the *pikeach* lifted only for himself. It then explains why two *chereshim* who lift a find together do acquire.

children.title: Rava's First Version: Both Acquire
children.gist: Rava rules that since the *cheresh* acquires, the *pikeach* acquires too. The Gemara objects that the *pikeach* can lift the *cheresh*'s half for him, but the *pikeach*'s half needs the *cheresh*, who can't acquire for another.

bullets.text: Rava: since we say *miggo*, a *cheresh* (a deaf-mute, who lacks legal competence) and a *pikeach* (a competent adult) who lift a found item together both acquire it: since the *cheresh* acquires, the *pikeach* acquires too.

The Gemara objects. The *cheresh*'s part is understood: the *pikeach*, acquiring his own part for himself, acquires the other part for the *cheresh*. But the *pikeach* needs the *cheresh* to acquire his part for him, and a *cheresh* can't acquire for another.
A *cheresh* has no *kinyan* by Torah law. The Sages let him keep a find for himself, to keep the peace, but that gives him no power to acquire for others.

children.title: Rava's Second Version: The *Cheresh* Acquires Alone
children.gist: The Gemara restates Rava: the *cheresh* acquires and the *pikeach* doesn't. The *miggo* is now a different one: since two *chereshim* who lift a find together acquire it, so does a *cheresh* who lifts it with a *pikeach*.

bullets.text: The Gemara restates Rava's ruling: the *cheresh* acquires his part, and the *pikeach* does not acquire his.

The *miggo* here is not that one who acquires for himself acquires for another. It is that since two *chereshim* who lift a find together acquire it, a *cheresh* lifting with a *pikeach* acquires too, even though the *pikeach* doesn't.

children.title: Neither Acquires, Since the *Pikeach* Lifted Only for Himself
children.gist: The Gemara rejects the second version: even Rami bar Chama's rule needs intent to acquire for the other, and a *pikeach* who gets nothing has no reason to lift for the *cheresh*. So neither acquires. Two *chereshim* differ, since the Sages let them acquire so they won't quarrel, while this *cheresh* won't quarrel when even the *pikeach* gets nothing.

bullets.text: The Gemara objects: even by Rami bar Chama, lifting for another works only where one intends the other to acquire. This *pikeach* lifted the item to acquire it for himself. If he gets nothing for himself, would he acquire for others?
So the conclusion: since the *pikeach* acquires nothing, the *cheresh* acquires nothing either.

Why are two *chereshim* different? There the Sages enacted that they acquire, so that they won't come to quarrel with anyone who tries to take the find from them. Here the *cheresh* says to himself: if even the *pikeach* doesn't acquire, can I? So he won't quarrel, and no enactment is needed.
The enactment answers a sense of injustice. Two *chereshim* robbed of a joint find would feel wronged; a *cheresh* who sees his competent partner lose as well has no grievance.

sections.title: Where in the Mishnah Rami bar Chama Finds His Proof
sections.gist: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda asks Rav Ashi which clause of the Mishnah shows that two who lift a find together both acquire. The Gemara tries the clauses in turn, and each turns out to teach something else, until the last: when the parties agree or have witnesses, they divide without an oath. Rava reads even that clause as *miggo*.

chart.title: Which clause of the garment Mishnah shows that two who lift a find together both acquire?
rows: Two hold a garment, each saying “I found it”
It is the basic case of two holding a find
Each claims he lifted all of it, so nothing implies lifting together
Both say “All of it is mine”
It seems to repeat the first case
It is a purchase, each saying he bought it (2a)
“All of it is mine” vs. “Half of it is mine”
It seems to add nothing
It may be a purchase: the one claiming half is not a *meshiv aveidah* and still swears
Two sitting on an animal
It seems to add nothing to the garment
That *rokhev* acquires, though the animal hasn't moved
They agree or have witnesses: divide without an oath
In a purchase this would be obvious
Nothing else: it must be a find lifted together, and the proof stands (Rava: by *miggo*)

children.title: Not the First Clause: Each Says He Lifted It All
children.gist: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda asks Rav Ashi where Rami bar Chama's inference lies. It can't be the opening case, since there each claims he lifted the whole garment himself.

bullets.text: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda asks Rav Ashi: from where in the Mishnah does Rami bar Chama draw his inference?
Not from the opening case of two holding a garment. There each says, “All of it is mine, and I lifted all of it,” so nothing there implies that they lifted it together.

children.title: Both Say “All of It Is Mine”: A Case of Buying
children.gist: The second “all of it is mine” case seems to repeat the first, and so might teach that two who lift a find at once divide it. The Gemara answers that it isn't extra: it was already explained as a dispute over a purchase.

bullets.text: Perhaps from the next case, where both say “All of it is mine.” It seems to repeat the first case, so it should teach that even two who lift a find at once divide it, and no third party may take it.
The Gemara answers that the clause isn't extra: it was already explained (2a) that the first case is a find and this one a purchase, with each saying he is the one who bought it.

children.title: “All of It Is Mine” vs. “Half of It Is Mine”: Why the Half-Claimant Still Swears
children.gist: Perhaps the case of one claiming all and the other half is extra, and teaches lifting together. The Gemara answers that it may speak of a purchase and teach that the one claiming half is not a *meshiv aveidah* exempt from an oath, since he may be scheming to avoid the oath.

bullets.text: Perhaps from the case where one says “All of it is mine” and the other “Half of it is mine”: what does it add, unless it teaches that two who lift together acquire?

The Gemara answers that it may speak of a purchase and still teach something. One might think the one claiming half is like a *meshiv aveidah* (one who returns a lost item), who is trusted without an oath: he could have claimed it all and instead conceded half.
The Mishnah teaches that he still swears, since he may be scheming: “If I say all of it is mine, I must swear. I'll say half, look like one returning a lost item, and be exempt.”
The concession is real: claiming all would have won him half, while claiming half wins him a quarter. That is why one might have trusted him.

children.title: Two Sitting on an Animal: Perhaps It Teaches That *Rokhev* Acquires
children.gist: The case of two sitting on an animal seems to add nothing, and so might be the source. The Gemara answers that it may teach that sitting on an animal acquires it, even though the animal hasn't moved.

bullets.text: Perhaps from the case of two sitting on an animal, each claiming it: it seems to add nothing to the garment, so it might teach that one who lifts a find for another acquires it for him.

The Gemara answers: it may teach that *rokhev* (sitting on an animal in a riding position) acquires it, even though the animal hasn't moved. That isn't obvious, since an animal is normally acquired by *meshikhah* (pulling it, so that it moves).

children.title: Agreement or Witnesses: They Divide Because They Lifted It Together
children.gist: The last clause has them divide without an oath when they agree or have witnesses. In a purchase that would be obvious, so it must speak of a find lifted together, and Rami bar Chama's proof stands. Rava reads this clause too as *miggo*.

bullets.text: Rami bar Chama's source is the last clause: when the parties admit each other's claims or have witnesses, they divide without an oath.

In a purchase that would go without saying. So it must speak of a find that they knowingly lifted together, each intending both to acquire, and they divide it: one who lifts a find for another acquires it for him.
Rava answers that this clause too rests on *miggo*: since each acquires for himself, he acquires for the other as well.
So Rava agrees with Rami bar Chama about the Mishnah itself. They differ only on one who lifts a find solely for another, at the expense of everyone else who might have taken it.

returns_to.note: Rava's *miggo* answer, now applied to the clause that proves joint acquisition

sections.title: Riding vs. Leading: Which Acts Acquire an Animal
sections.gist: Rav Yehuda heard from Shmuel that of *rokhev* and *manhig*, one acquires and the other doesn't, but forgot which. The Gemara reads his question as one riding while another leads, and Rav Yehuda tries to settle it from the one sitting in a wagon in *kilayim* (the prohibition of working diverse kinds together). The Gemara rules that holding the reins acquires only when they are handed over, and explains the Mishnah's rider as one who drives with his legs.

chart.title: Which act acquires an animal, as the Gemara works it out here
rows: *Manhig*: leading or pulling it
**Acquires**
The animal walks because of him: it is *meshikhah*
*Rokhev* alone, by Rav Yehuda's proof
**Does not acquire**
Sitting is no act, as Shmuel's version of the wagon-sitter in *kilayim* shows
Taking the reins from a seller
**Acquires**
*Mesirah*: the owner hands the reins over
Holding the reins of a found or ownerless animal
**Does not acquire**
No one hands them over, and merely holding them is no act
Riding while driving with the legs
**Acquires**, equal to leading
A second kind of *manhig*, no stronger than leading by the reins

sections.continues: Continues at 8b.13: the Gemara brings a baraita on pulling a camel and driving a donkey to test whether riding acquires.

children.title: Rav Yehuda's Forgotten Ruling: A Rider Against a Leader
children.gist: Rav Yehuda couldn't remember which of Shmuel's two rulings applied to riding and which to leading. Since leading alone surely acquires, the Gemara concludes the question was one sitting on the animal while another leads it: does the rider win because he holds it, or the leader because it walks on his account?

bullets.text: The Mishnah: if two were sitting on an animal, or one sat on it while the other led it, each swears and they divide it.

Rav Yosef reports that Rav Yehuda told him: I heard two rulings from Shmuel, one on *rokhev* and one on *manhig* (leading or driving the animal). One acquires and the other doesn't, but I don't know which is which.
The Gemara asks how he could be unsure. Who says that leading an animal alone doesn't acquire? It is a classic act of acquisition. If either one fails, it is obviously sitting.
So his question must have been one sitting on the animal while another leads it. Does the rider take precedence, since his legs grasp the animal, or the leader, since it walks because of him?
The shiur distinguishes a rider who drives the animal, which shades into leading, from one merely seated on it; the doubt concerns the static seat.

children.title: Rav Yehuda's Proof: The One Sitting in the Wagon in *Kilayim*
children.gist: In the Mishnah in Kilayim, both the one leading mixed animals and the one sitting in their wagon get lashes, while R. Meir exempts the sitter. Shmuel taught it reversed, with the Rabbis exempting the sitter, so Rav Yehuda concludes that sitting on an animal does not acquire it, and surely not against a leader.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda tries to work it out from a Mishnah (Kilayim 8:3): when two animals of different kinds, such as a horse and a donkey, are harnessed to one wagon, the one leading them gets 40 lashes for “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together” (Devarim 22:10), and so does the one sitting in the wagon. R. Meir exempts the sitter, since he did nothing.
Shmuel taught it reversed: the Rabbis exempt the one sitting in the wagon. That shows he held this view, since the halakha follows the Rabbis against R. Meir: sitting is not a significant act.
So sitting on an animal alone does not acquire it, and all the more so when someone else is leading it.

Tosafot supplies the bridge from lashes to *kinyan*: sitting moves the animal a little, so it could count as a form of *meshikhah*. If moving the animals that way isn't driving them for *kilayim*, it isn't *meshikhah* for acquisition either.

children.title: A Wagon-Sitter Doesn't Hold the Reins, but Holding Them Acquires Nothing
children.gist: Abaye questions whether Rav Yosef really heard this proof from Rav Yehuda. Rav Yosef recalls the exchange: he objected that a rider holds the reins while a wagon-sitter doesn't, and Rav Yehuda answered that holding the reins of an ownerless animal doesn't acquire. In another version Abaye objects and Rav Yosef answers from Idi's baraita.

bullets.text: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef: many times you told us “let us see” and brought this proof, without saying it came from Rav Yehuda. Rav Yosef had suffered an illness that made him forget, and Abaye suspected the attribution was mistaken.

Rav Yosef: I do remember Rav Yehuda saying it, and I remember objecting: how can you learn one sitting on an animal from one sitting in a wagon? The wagon-sitter doesn't hold the reins, while the rider does.
Rav Yehuda answered: Rav and Shmuel both say that holding the reins of an ownerless animal does not acquire it. So the rider has nothing more than the wagon-sitter.
Another version: Abaye himself raised the objection about the reins, and Rav Yosef answered with a baraita taught by Idi: holding the reins of an ownerless animal does not acquire it.
Sitting is no act, and holding the reins of an ownerless animal is no act, so together they still come to nothing.

children.title: *Mesirah* Acquires from a Seller, Not from Ownerless Property
children.gist: R. Chelbo, in the name of Rav Huna, rules that taking the reins acquires an animal from another person, but not a find or a convert's estate. Rava explains in Idi's name that the reins are named for handing over, and an ownerless animal has no one to hand them over.

bullets.text: R. Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna: *mesirah* (taking hold of the reins) acquires an animal from another person, but not a found animal, or one from the estate of a convert who died without heirs, which is ownerless.

Rava, as Idi explained to him: the word for reins, *moseirah*, comes from *moser*, one who hands an item over to another. From a seller it works, because he hands them over; with a find or a convert's estate no one hands them over, and merely holding them acquires nothing.
The force of *mesirah* lies in the act of transfer, not in the grip.

children.title: The Mishnah's Rider Drives with His Legs: Two Kinds of *Manhig*
children.gist: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah's riders: by R. Meir the Mishnah would have taught the wagon-sitter, so it follows the Rabbis, and riding acquires. It answers that the rider drives the animal with his legs, a second kind of *manhig*, and the Mishnah teaches that it is no stronger than leading by the reins, so they divide.

bullets.text: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: two sitting on an animal, or one sitting and one leading, divide it. Whose view is that? Not R. Meir's: if even one sitting in a wagon acquires, the Mishnah needn't teach a rider. So it is the Rabbis', and *rokhev* acquires.
Answer: the Mishnah's rider also leads, driving the animal by squeezing or kicking it with his legs.

Then he is simply leading, so why teach it? The *tanna* teaches two kinds of *manhig*: pulling by the reins, and driving from the saddle. One might think the rider wins, since he both drives the animal and holds it; the Mishnah teaches that his claim is no stronger than the leader's, so they divide.
This answers Shmuel's question in its own terms: when both act at once, neither the hold nor the pull outweighs the other.

returns_to.note: Answers the question of a rider against a leader

key_terms.definition: Acquiring a movable object by lifting it; it acquires both ownerless objects and items bought from another.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Two who lift a garment together each lift only part, which raises whether each can acquire the other's part for him.

key_terms.sense: acquiring a benefit for someone in his absence
key_terms.definition: The principle that one may acquire something on another person's behalf without his knowledge, since it is to his benefit.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Taking a find for another shuts out third parties, so Rami bar Chama's ruling goes beyond this principle.

key_terms.sense: “since”: one legal result carrying another with it
key_terms.definition: An argument of the form “since this holds, that holds too”: because a person stands in one legal position, a related result follows.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava holds that one who acquires part of a find for himself acquires the other part for his partner; the Gemara also tries a *miggo* from two *chereshim*.

key_terms.definition: The rule that an agent's sinful act is not attributed to the one who sent him; the agent alone is responsible.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava contrasts the exempt sender of a thief with partners who steal together and are both liable.

key_terms.definition: A deaf-mute, who in halakha lacks legal competence and so cannot perform a Torah-law *kinyan*; the Sages let him acquire a find for the sake of peace.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks whether a *cheresh* who lifts a find with a *pikeach* acquires, and concludes neither does, unlike two *chereshim*.

key_terms.definition: A person of sound mind and full legal capacity, as opposed to a *cheresh* (deaf-mute), a *shoteh* (a person with psychosis) or a minor.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A *pikeach* who lifts a find with a *cheresh* acquires nothing, since the *cheresh* can't acquire for him, and so he lifts nothing for the *cheresh*.

key_terms.sense: one who returns a lost item
key_terms.definition: One who returns a lost object he could have kept; he is trusted and is exempt from an oath about it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The one claiming only half the garment might have been treated as one, but the Mishnah has him swear, since he may be scheming.

key_terms.sense: sitting on an animal as a mode of acquisition
key_terms.definition: Sitting on an animal in a riding position; whether this acquires the animal, without its being moved, is debated.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Yehuda proves from the wagon-sitter that sitting alone doesn't acquire; the Gemara reads the Mishnah's rider as one who also drives the animal.

key_terms.definition: Leading or driving an animal so that it walks because of him; a form of *meshikhah* that acquires the animal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara counts two kinds, pulling by the reins and driving from the saddle with the legs, and rules that neither outweighs the other.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring a movable object, such as an animal, by pulling or moving it; the standard act of acquisition for animals.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Leading is plainly *meshikhah*, which is why Rav Yehuda's doubt must concern a rider and a leader at once.

key_terms.sense: acquiring an animal by taking its reins
key_terms.definition: Acquiring an animal by taking hold of its reins or halter when the owner hands them over.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It acquires from a seller but not a found animal or a convert's estate, since there no one hands the reins over.

key_terms.sense: working animals of diverse kinds together
key_terms.definition: The Torah prohibition of plowing or drawing with two animals of different kinds harnessed together.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The dispute over whether one sitting in a wagon drawn by mixed animals is lashed serves as a test of whether sitting is a significant act.

sages.name: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda

quiz.q: Two people lift a found garment together, each holding one end. Why does Rami bar Chama say that, if lifting for another didn't work, neither would acquire it?
options: Each lifted only his part, so the other part would count as still lying on the ground
Each claims the whole garment, so their claims cancel out
A found item is acquired only by one who lifts it alone
Two people can never share ownership of a found item
quiz.why: *Hagbahah* must take in the whole object. Since the Mishnah has them divide it, each must be lifting the other's part for him.

quiz.q: A man lifts a found item intending only that his friend acquire it, wanting nothing himself. What does Rava hold?
options: The friend does not acquire it; acquiring for another works only *miggo* one acquires for himself
The friend acquires it, by *zakhin le'adam she'lo be'fanav*
The lifter acquires it himself, whatever he intended
It stays ownerless until the friend lifts it himself, and the lifter must return it to its place
quiz.why: Rava reads the Mishnah as *miggo*: each acquires the other's part only because he is acquiring his own part for himself.

quiz.q: Two partners steal an item, and only one of them lifts it. Unlike a man who sends an agent to steal, both are liable. Why?
options: Since the one who lifts it acquires for himself, he acquires for his partner too
Partners are each other's agents even for a transgression
The partner who didn't lift it is liable for planning the theft
Theft by partners is a rabbinic penalty
quiz.why: *Ein shaliach li'dvar aveirah* exempts the sender of an agent, but a partner's act for himself carries the other along.

quiz.q: A *cheresh* and a *pikeach* lift a found item together. What does the Gemara conclude?
options: Neither acquires it
Both acquire it, as two *chereshim* would
Only the *cheresh* acquires, by the Sages' enactment
Only the *pikeach* acquires, since a *cheresh* has no *kinyan*
quiz.why: The *cheresh* can't acquire for the *pikeach*, and a *pikeach* who gets nothing for himself doesn't lift for the *cheresh*.

quiz.q: Two *chereshim* lift a found item together. Why do they acquire it, when a *cheresh* lifting with a *pikeach* does not?
options: The Sages enacted it so they won't quarrel; with a *pikeach* who also loses, the *cheresh* won't quarrel
Two *chereshim* together count as one competent person
Each *cheresh* can acquire for the other by Torah law
A *pikeach* cancels the *cheresh*'s acquisition by objecting
quiz.why: The enactment exists to prevent quarrels, and a *cheresh* who sees that even the *pikeach* gets nothing has no reason to fight.

quiz.q: Two hold a garment; one says “All of it is mine” and the other “Half of it is mine.” Why must the one claiming half also swear?
options: He may be scheming to look like a *meshiv aveidah* and so escape the oath
A partial claim always requires an oath by Torah law
He admitted part, so he is a *modeh be'miktzat*
His claim is suspect because he holds only half
quiz.why: He might reason that claiming all brings an oath, while claiming half makes him look like one returning a lost item.

quiz.q: Someone takes hold of the reins of a found, ownerless donkey. According to R. Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna, does he acquire it?
options: No: *mesirah* acquires only when an owner hands the reins over
Yes: holding the reins is a full *kinyan* for any animal
Yes, but only if he also sits on it
No, unless he leads it at least the length of the animal
quiz.why: As Idi explained, *moseirah* comes from handing over; with an ownerless animal no one hands it over, and merely holding the reins acquires nothing.

quiz.q: One person sits on a donkey and drives it with his legs while another leads it by the reins, and each claims it. What does the Mishnah teach, as the Gemara explains it?
options: They divide it: both are forms of *manhig*, and the rider's is no stronger
The rider takes it, since he both drives and holds it
The leader takes it, since the donkey walks because of him
Neither acquires, since sitting is not a *kinyan*
quiz.why: The *tanna* teaches two kinds of *manhig*, and the rider's hold doesn't give him precedence over the leader.

judgment_calls: Rava's *cheresh* and *pikeach* discussion (8a.8–13) is nested under the Rami bar Chama section rather than set apart, since it is Rava's application of the *miggo* mechanism he introduces there; its three versions are children, as each revision answers the one before.

The search for Rami bar Chama's source in the Mishnah (8a.14–23) is a top-level section of its own: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda opens a new exchange, and its last step, Rava's *miggo* reading, is linked back to s3 with returns_to.
The two versions of the Abaye–Rav Yosef exchange (8b.6–8) are kept in one section, since both reach the same point: holding the reins of an ownerless animal doesn't acquire.
The ruling on *mesirah* (8b.9–10) is a child of the riding section rather than its own top-level section, since the Gemara brings it as support for the reply about the reins.
The Mishnah's riders (8b.11–12) close the riding section with a returns_to link to Rav Yehuda's question, since the answer settles a rider against a leader.
coverage_notes: 8a.1–3 (division as division of value) belongs to the previous daf's outline and was covered at the end of the previous shiur.
The essay describes the partners who steal as each carrying part of the item; the text says both are liable even if only one of them lifted it. Followed the text.

The essay explains the second version (8a.10) as the *cheresh* acquiring because the *pikeach* lifts for him; the text grounds it in a different *miggo*: since two *chereshim* who lift together acquire. Followed the text.

The essay explains the difference from two *chereshim* by fairness between the parties; the text says the *cheresh* himself won't quarrel when even the *pikeach* gets nothing. Followed the text, keeping the essay's framing as a shiur bullet.
The essay has Rava conclude that the agent and partner cases must be kept distinct; the text concludes simply that the *miggo* principle is correct. Followed the text.

The essay attributes the reins teaching to Idi and the objection to Abaye; the text gives two versions: in the first, Rav Yosef objected to Rav Yehuda, who answered in the name of Rav and Shmuel; in the second, Abaye objected and Rav Yosef answered from Idi's baraita. The text also has Abaye question the attribution to Rav Yehuda because of Rav Yosef's illness. Followed the text.
The essay speaks of an ox and a donkey in the *kilayim* case; the text's example of the harnessed pair is a horse and a donkey, citing the ox-and-donkey verse. Followed the text.
The shiur's discussion of the baraita on pulling a camel and driving a donkey (8b.13 onward), if any, falls outside this outline's scope.

charts.subject: Agent sent to steal vs. partners who steal
charts.why_not: Only two cases with one reason each; the illustration shows them side by side.

charts.subject: The *kilayim* Mishnah as we have it vs. Shmuel's version
charts.why_not: A simple reversal of two names; the bullets carry it clearly.

charts.subject: The rider's claim vs. the leader's claim
charts.why_not: One sentence each; the s19 illustration puts both claims in speech bubbles.

illustrations.why_not: The point is a legal inference from lashes, and a sixth scene would repeat the riding picture without a new case.

daf_summary.summary: Discussion of: whether one who lifts a found item for another acquires it for him (Rami bar Chama: yes; Rava: only by *miggo*, as with partners who steal), and a *cheresh* and a *pikeach* who lift a find together (neither acquires); which clause of the garment Mishnah proves joint acquisition (the case of agreement or witnesses); and riding against leading as acts that acquire an animal (Rav Yehuda's proof from the wagon-sitter, *mesirah* of the reins, and the rider who drives with his legs).

takeaways.text: Two who lift a find together each acquire half: by Rami bar Chama because one can lift a find for another, by Rava only because each, acquiring for himself, acquires for his partner too.
Partners who steal are both liable even when only one lifts the item, while one who sends an agent to steal is exempt, since there is no agency for a transgression.

When a *cheresh* and a *pikeach* lift a find together, neither acquires: the *cheresh* can't acquire for the *pikeach*, and a *pikeach* who gets nothing lifts nothing for the *cheresh*. Two *chereshim* do acquire, by an enactment against quarrels.
The one who claims only half the garment still swears, since he may be posing as a *meshiv aveidah* to escape the oath.

Holding the reins acquires an animal only when a seller hands them over, not a find or a convert's estate; and a rider who drives with his legs is a second kind of *manhig*, no stronger than one who leads by the reins, so they divide.

debates.question: Can one who lifts a found item solely for another acquire it for him?

sides.view: Yes: two who lift together each acquire the other's part for him
No: two who lift together acquire only by *miggo*, since each acquires for himself

debates.question: When one sits on an animal and another leads it, who acquires it?

sides.view: He takes precedence, since his legs grasp the animal
He takes precedence, since the animal walks because of him

debates.outcome: The Mishnah's rider drives with his legs, a second kind of *manhig*, and is no stronger than the leader, so they divide.

debates.question: Is one who sits in a wagon drawn by mixed animals lashed for *kilayim*?

sides.view: Yes, like the one leading them
No, since he did nothing; Shmuel taught this as the Rabbis' view

debates.outcome: Since Shmuel exempts the sitter, Rav Yehuda concludes that sitting on an animal does not acquire it.
